feed.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay

entry.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay
entry.summary: The `staletip` proposal presents a significant advancement in the observability and analysis of stale rates within the Bitcoin network. Stale blocks, which arise when two valid blocks are found nearly simultaneously at the same height, have historically been difficult to monitor due to rapid block propagation technologies such as compact block relay and FIBRE. These technologies tend to suppress the visibility of stale branches unless a node is specifically monitoring for them. By introducing an optional peer-to-peer (P2P) messaging system, `staletip` allows participating nodes to share data about recently observed stale tips with others who have opted into this feature. The collaborative development of this protocol, building on the work of AJ Towns and furthered by pseudoramdom and w0xlt, has produced a [Draft BIP](https://github.com/pseudoramdom/bips/blob/staletip-bip-draft/bip-staletip.md) and associated [proof-of-concept implementation](https://github.com/w0xlt/bitcoin/tree/staletip-v4). Technically, `staletip` leverages the BIP 434 `feature` message to signal support among nodes. Each staletip message includes details on the fork point, a sequence of up to 20 compressed headers, and a flag indicating if the sender can supply the corresponding stale tip block. To reduce potential network load and irrelevant data sharing, information exchange is limited to tips within 1000 blocks of the active chain tip, and each node maintains a cache of up to ten recent tips. This design aims to facilitate more rapid detection of network partitions, adversarial mining strategies, or block propagation delays, ultimately supporting improved diagnostics and handling of blockchain reorganizations. A parallel effort focuses on documenting mainnet stale blocks through continuous monitoring with long-running nodes, given that stale blocks cannot be easily recovered from the network post-facto. This monitoring initiative is open to review and contribution via [this repository](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/stale-blocks). While beneficial for research and transparency, concerns exist regarding increased vulnerability to denial-of-service (DoS) and fingerprinting attacks, as well as challenges in representing multiple competing chains—especially relevant in signet and testnets where forks are common. The current system primarily handles a single branch per message, which could be insufficient under more complex forking scenarios. These limitations underscore the need for ongoing refinement, balancing enhanced transparency against potential security risks and operational complexity. Security considerations, particularly regarding DoS and fingerprinting, have been rigorously discussed. Relaying small messages does not introduce new vectors for resource exhaustion, as constraints like branch-length, recency, and cache limits effectively bound resource usage. Invalid data transmission as an attack vector is already possible in the existing network; the proposed changes do not amplify this risk. Nodes remain free to enforce stricter controls or disable features deemed problematic. Regarding fingerprinting, enabling staletip introduces a detectable feature, a trade-off typical for opt-in P2P functionalities. Operators concerned about this aspect retain full discretion to disable the relay of staletip data. The proposal assumes distinct announcements for each competing chain, ensuring clear communication of linear branches and their respective fork points and headers. From a protocol evolution standpoint, a cautious and incremental approach is recommended. Initially, relaying only stale headers—not full block data—is advocated as it provides most of the desired transparency benefits without significantly disturbing mining incentives or the broader incentive structure. Transmitting only headers enhances the ability to detect stale blocks and supports faster reorganization without exposing sensitive transaction-level data or pool attribution, which could alter miner behavior. Comprehensive incentive analysis for header-only relay appears unnecessary, given the minimal impact compared to full block relay. Only after evaluating the results of this change should expansion to relaying full blocks be considered, always weighing potential shifts in mining dynamics. The reference implementation offers three operational modes: disabling stale relay entirely, relaying only stale headers, or relaying full stale blocks. The default is set to none, but configuration options provide flexibility according to network policy or operator preference. Arguments against making full block relay the default, or even a supported option, cite the minimal impact on mining incentives. Any benefit from faster stale block relay can be replicated privately by miners, and the primary driver of mining decisions remains the highest cumulative proof-of-work rather than stale blocks. Relay improvements affect only marginal aspects of block validation speed and reorganization response. Practical benefits of relaying stale blocks at the current tip’s height include increased network awareness of all mined blocks, thereby dispelling suspicions of block withholding during reorganizations and improving detection of double-spends or censorship events. Empirical data from past reorganizations demonstrates that rapid propagation of stale block contents would serve to clarify honest behavior and mitigate unfounded allegations of selfish mining. Moreover, withholding stale block relay may inadvertently advantage attackers who deploy proprietary relay infrastructure, suggesting that open propagation strengthens the honest network's position.
